summary: Sets out requirements for the protocol between path computation clients and path computation elements, and for discovering them, when traffic engineering spans several network layers such as MPLS and GMPLS layers. Planning end to end across layers can make the whole network more efficient. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A trip may use a train, then a bus. Planning it together beats planning each alone. This lists what network route planners need to plan across layers.

questions: what is pce inter-layer traffic engineering
how can a pce see multiple network layers
what is a virtual network topology
subtitle: How to plan routes across multiple network layers efficiently.

tldr.problem: Large networks have multiple layers (packet networks, optical networks, etc.), but routers in one layer often cannot see the topology of other layers, making it impossible to plan end-to-end efficient routes.
tldr.mechanism: The Path Computation Element (PCE) can compute routes that span multiple layers by having access to all layer topologies or by cooperating with other PCEs that each know one layer, and the communication protocol must support passing constraints and layer-specific information between the client and PCE.
tldr.outcome: Networks can achieve better resource utilization by optimizing across all layers at once, rather than optimizing each layer independently.

facts.label: Cooperation mode
facts.value: Single PCE or multiple cooperating PCEs

today: RFC 6457 is an Informational RFC that sets out requirements for standardized implementations of inter-layer path computation. While it does not define the protocol itself, it is the basis for protocol extensions in standards such as the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP) that are used in modern software-defined networking and optical network deployments.

sections.title: Multiple Layers in Modern Networks
sections.content:
Large networks are built in layers. A high layer might be a packet network (IP/MPLS) running on top of a lower layer that is an optical network controlled by GMPLS. In some networks, there are even more layers: different switching types like packet switching (PSC), time division multiplex (TDM), or lambda switching (LSC).

Each layer carries traffic for the layers above it. For example, an IP packet might travel through several routers in the packet layer, but its actual path across the optical layer is carried by one or more optical circuits.

The challenge is that a router in the high-layer network often does not know the topology of the layers below. An IP router in the packet network might not be able to see which optical circuits exist or how the optical network is connected. This makes it impossible for the IP router to plan an end-to-end path that uses resources efficiently across both layers.
sections.eli5: A big network may have layers: one layer for packets, one for optical signals. A router in the packet layer does not see the optical layer, so it cannot plan a trip that uses both well.

sections.title: Why Multi-Layer Route Planning Matters
sections.content:
Suppose two cities are connected by an optical network, with border routers in each city that can send IP packets. An IP router in one city wants to send packets to the other city, but it does not know whether there are any TE (Traffic Engineering) links in the IP layer between the border routers. If the IP router tries to route the path using only what it knows, it fails.

However, a Path Computation Element (PCE) can be given a view of both the IP layer and the optical layer. The PCE can see that while there is no direct IP link between the border routers, it is possible to set up an optical circuit between them. The PCE can then suggest a path in the IP layer that goes to a border router, suggests establishing a lower-layer optical circuit, and exits at the other border router.

This kind of inter-layer path computation allows the network to make better use of its resources. By considering all layers at once, a network operator can build paths that are more efficient or that serve more traffic than would be possible if each layer were optimized independently.
sections.eli5: A route planner that knows both layers can say "use the packet network here, set up an optical circuit here, then use the packet network again". Doing it layer by layer would not find this route.

sections.title: Communication Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol between a Path Computation Client (PCC, typically a router or management system) and a Path Computation Element must support several new capabilities for inter-layer work.

First, a PCC must be able to tell a PCE whether inter-layer path computation is allowed, or whether it wants only a single-layer path. The PCE must also be able to tell the PCC whether the path it computed requires triggered signaling (setting up lower-layer paths automatically when the upper-layer path is signaled), since this can increase setup latency.

Second, the PCC and PCE must be able to exchange constraints about which layers are allowed, which switching types are acceptable, and how many layer boundaries can be crossed. Different layers may need different optimization objectives: the packet layer might be optimized for minimum delay, while the optical layer might be optimized for fewest hops.

Third, when multiple PCEs are involved (one PCE for each layer), the protocol must allow them to cooperate. A PCE in the higher layer might ask a PCE in the lower layer to compute a path, and the lower-layer PCE might ask the upper-layer PCE to check constraints or verify that a path is feasible.

Fourth, the PCE must be able to report the type of path it computed (single-layer or multi-layer), and when a multi-layer path is returned, it must include the paths of any lower-layer circuits that need to be established.
sections.eli5: The route planner and the network element asking for a route need to talk about which layers to use, what rules to follow, whether to set up circuits automatically, and whether the planner should ask other planners for help.

sections.title: Discovering PCE Capabilities
sections.content:
When a network has multiple PCEs with different capabilities, a PCC needs to know which PCE can do what. A PCE discovery mechanism must be able to advertise several things: whether it supports inter-layer path computation, whether it can compute both single-layer and multi-layer paths, whether it understands inter-layer constraints, and whether it can cooperate with other PCEs.

A PCE might also advertise support for diverse path computation: the ability to compute multiple paths between the same two points that are diverse at each layer (meaning they do not share links, nodes, or risk groups). This is useful for backup and recovery planning.

The discovery mechanism should also allow a PCE to advertise which architectural models it supports. Some networks use an overlay model where the higher layer and lower layer are managed separately. Others use an integrated model where they are tightly coupled, or an augmented model where a single management plane controls both layers.
sections.eli5: When asking for a route, you need to know if the planner can do multi-layer planning, or if it only knows one layer. The planner advertises what it can do.

sections.title: Management and Policy
sections.content:
A PCE can be configured to support inter-layer computation or to keep that capability hidden. This is useful for security or policy reasons: an operator might want only certain trusted clients to know that inter-layer computation is available.

All extensions to the communication protocol must be accompanied by MIB objects (management information bases) that allow network operators to control and monitor the PCE and the inter-layer computations it performs.

When a PCC makes a request that is forwarded between multiple PCEs, the original PCC and the first PCE cannot directly monitor the health of all the intermediate PCE connections. However, each PCE in the chain should monitor the connections it uses and report failures back to the original request so the PCC can know whether the computation succeeded or failed.

The topology graph that the PCE uses to plan paths must include information about the inter-layer forwarding and adaptation capabilities of each router in the network. This information is usually distributed using extensions to routing protocols such as OSPF-TE or IS-IS-TE.
sections.eli5: Operators need to be able to turn inter-layer planning on or off, and to monitor whether the route planner is working. Each planner needs to know the capabilities of the routers it is planning for.
